topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Blood opens the B2 Foundation paper more often than not: Summer 2025 Q1 was 7 marks (three components matched to functions [3], then nucleus, biconcave, iron and a plasma substance [1] each) and Summer 2024 Q2 was 5 marks. Vessels come back later in the same paper attached to the heart — Summer 2025 Higher Q1(b) asked for two vessel types and only [1] of the [2] was usually earned. Summer 2022 Higher Q1(b) was a five-row tick table on vessel features worth [6]. Cell lysis is Higher only and has appeared in Unit 7 Booklet B.
mustMemorise: Red cells: biconcave, no nucleus, haemoglobin containing iron — they carry oxygen
White cells defend the body against disease. Platelets turn fibrinogen into fibrin, so the blood clots and a scab forms
Plasma transports cells, food molecules, carbon dioxide, hormones and urea — not oxygen
Artery: thick wall with muscle and elastic fibres, small lumen, high pressure, away from the heart
Vein: thin wall, large lumen, low pressure, towards the heart, valves prevent backflow
Capillary: wall one cell thick and permeable, for exchange with the tissues
Higher: red blood cells in water take in water by osmosis and burst — lysis
Magnification = drawn size ÷ real size, in the same unit
notOnThisSpec: The clotting cascade beyond fibrinogen to fibrin
Arterioles, venules and the structure of the three wall layers by name

sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Blood often opens the Foundation paper, with a matching exercise worth [3] and then single [1] recall lines — nucleus, biconcave, iron, a substance in the plasma. Vessels appear both on their own (a tick table worth up to [6]) and attached to the heart question, where naming the vessel type is [1] each. Cell lysis is Higher only. The accept lists are tight: 'biconcave' not 'round', 'capillary' not 'small vein'.
traps: Not linking platelets to both of their functions (Summer 2025 B2 Foundation Q1)
Giving 'round' or 'flat' instead of 'biconcave' (Summer 2025 B2 Foundation Q1)
Being unable to give the function or the adaptations of a red blood cell (Summer 2024 B2 Foundation Q2)
Giving oxygen as a substance transported by the plasma (Summer 2023 B2 Foundation Q2)
Naming a function of a component when the question asks what the plasma carries (Summer 2023 B2 Foundation Q2)
Not naming the vessel of exchange as a capillary (Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q1)
Swapping the artery's and the vein's wall thickness and lumen size
Calling a red blood cell in water 'turgid' instead of burst (Summer 2023 Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Higher Q4)
Dividing millimetres by micrometres in a magnification

noteBlocks.text: Blood is four parts, each with a job

noteBlocks.md: Spin a tube of blood and it separates, as in the drawing: a pale, straw-coloured liquid on top, the **plasma**, and the cells packed underneath. A thin pale band between them holds the **white cells** and **platelets**; the dark layer below is **red cells**.

Each part has one job. **Red cells** carry oxygen. **White cells** defend the body against disease. **Platelets** convert **fibrinogen** into **fibrin**, which makes the blood clot, so a cut stops bleeding and a scab forms. The **plasma** carries everything else, dissolved.

noteBlocks.stem: A blood test shows that Aoife has far fewer platelets than normal. Suggest what will happen when she cuts her finger. [2]

steps.working: Platelets convert fibrinogen into fibrin, which makes the blood clot.
steps.decision: Start from the job of the part she is short of: naming what platelets do is the first mark.

steps.working: With fewer platelets, less fibrin forms, so her blood clots more slowly and the cut bleeds for longer before a scab forms.
steps.decision: Then apply that job to her: less of it gets done. Say what that means for the cut itself.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Blood"
noteBlocks.why: A second pass over the parts of blood and their jobs, after the worked answer. Watch it, then answer the next check without going back.

noteBlocks.prompt: A blood test shows far fewer white blood cells than normal. What is most likely?
options: Infections are harder to fight off
Cuts take longer to stop bleeding
noteBlocks.answer: Infections are harder to fight off
noteBlocks.explain: Work it as the platelet answer did: name the job of the part that is short, then say what less of it means. White cells defend the body against disease, so with fewer of them infections are harder to fight off. Slow clotting belongs to platelets, and carrying oxygen to red cells.

optionNotes.option: Cuts take longer to stop bleeding
optionNotes.why: It tempts because a short blood part does cause a problem, but slow clotting comes from too few platelets, not too few white cells.
It tempts because any missing part sounds serious, but carrying oxygen is the red cells' job, so too few white cells leave it untouched.

twin.prompt: A blood test shows far fewer red blood cells than normal. What is most likely?
options: Infections are harder to fight off
Cuts take longer to stop bleeding
twin.explain: Red cells carry oxygen, so with fewer of them less oxygen reaches the muscles. Defence is the white cells' job and clotting the platelets'.

optionNotes.option: Infections are harder to fight off
optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is the result when white cells are low, but fighting infection is the white cells' job, and red cells carry oxygen.

optionNotes.option: Cuts take longer to stop bleeding
optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is another blood-test result, but clotting is the platelets' job, not the red cells'.

noteBlocks.md: The plasma is the liquid part of blood, mostly water, and it carries its cargo dissolved: **food molecules** such as amino acids from the gut, **carbon dioxide** from the tissues to the lungs, **hormones** from the glands that make them, and **urea** from the liver to the kidneys.

One thing it does **not** carry is **oxygen**: almost all of it is bound to haemoglobin inside the red cells. Summer 2023 examiners saw candidates put oxygen in the plasma, and others give the job of a blood part when a substance was asked for.

noteBlocks.stem: Name three substances, other than cells, that the plasma transports. [3]

steps.working: Carbon dioxide.
steps.decision: Carried from the respiring tissues to the lungs. Each substance named is one mark.

steps.working: Amino acids.
steps.decision: A food molecule, absorbed from the small intestine after digestion.

steps.working: Urea.
steps.decision: Carried from the liver to the kidneys. A wrong item beside a right one costs that line its mark, so name only what you are sure the plasma carries.

noteBlocks.finalAnswer: Carbon dioxide, amino acids and urea.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is NOT transported by the plasma?
noteBlocks.explain: The plasma carries dissolved substances: urea to the kidneys, hormones from the glands, carbon dioxide to the lungs. Oxygen is the exception, as step 3 of the worked answer warned: it is bound to haemoglobin inside the red cells. So oxygen is the one the plasma does not carry.

twin.prompt: Which of these does the plasma carry from the liver to the kidneys?
twin.explain: Urea is made in the liver and carried dissolved in the plasma to the kidneys. Oxygen rides in the red cells, and fibrin forms only where the blood clots.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because oxygen is the best-known thing blood carries, but it rides in the red cells, joined to haemoglobin, not dissolved in the plasma.
It tempts because fibrin comes from the blood, but it only forms, as threads, where a clot is made, and it is not carried to the kidneys.
It tempts because urea is a waste, but wastes travel dissolved in the plasma, and urea is carried in it from the liver to the kidneys.
It tempts because hormones act far from where they are made, but that journey is made dissolved in the plasma.

noteBlocks.text: A red cell built for oxygen

noteBlocks.alt: A field of view down a microscope showing dozens of round, purple-stained red blood cells packed closely together, each with a distinctly paler centre, and two small dark-stained specks between them.
noteBlocks.credit: U.S. Air Force photo/Airman 1st Class Laura Max., Wikimedia Commons, Public domain
noteBlocks.caption: A real smear. The pale centre of each cell is the dip in the middle of the disc; the two dark specks are platelets.
noteBlocks.prompt: Why does each red cell look paler in the middle than round the edge — and which adaptation does that pale centre show you?

noteBlocks.md: Down a microscope a red cell looks paler in the middle because it is a **biconcave** disc: dimpled on both sides, which gives a large surface area for taking up oxygen. It has **no nucleus**, leaving more room for **haemoglobin**, the red pigment that contains **iron** and binds oxygen.

A white cell is different in almost every way: it is larger, it has a nucleus, it has no haemoglobin, and it is not biconcave. Its nucleus may be one large round one or split into lobes. Summer 2023 asked for two of those differences.

noteBlocks.stem: In a blood smear, give two differences in structure between a white blood cell and a red blood cell. [2]

steps.working: A white blood cell has a nucleus; a red blood cell has none.
steps.decision: One difference per mark. Name both cells so it reads as a comparison: the scheme is written about the white cell, and a red-cell fact on its own counts only as a plain converse.

steps.working: A white blood cell has no haemoglobin; a red blood cell is packed with it.
steps.decision: A second, separate idea. Size would also do (a white cell is larger), and so would shape (a red cell is biconcave).

noteBlocks.prompt: In a stained smear, cell P is large and has a lobed nucleus; cell Q is a small disc with a paler centre. Which is the white blood cell?
noteBlocks.explain: Use the worked differences: a white cell has a nucleus and is the larger cell, while a red cell has no nucleus and its dimple makes a paler centre. P has the nucleus and the size, so P is the white blood cell.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because Q is the cell you see most, but a small disc with a pale centre and no nucleus is a red cell.
It tempts because both are blood cells, but only one of them has a nucleus, and the white cell is the one that does.

twin.prompt: In a smear, cell R is large with one round nucleus; cell S is a small pale-centred disc with no nucleus. Which is the red blood cell?
twin.explain: A red cell has no nucleus, and its biconcave dimple shows as a paler centre: that is S. R, with its nucleus, is a white cell.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because R shows the clearer features, but a nucleus and a large size mark a white cell.
It tempts because both are blood cells, but only S lacks a nucleus and shows the pale dimple of a red cell.

noteBlocks.caption: Pure water enters the red cell by osmosis; with no wall to stop it, the cell swells and bursts.

noteBlocks.title: Why a plant cell survives the same water
noteBlocks.md: A plant cell has a **cell wall** that will not stretch, so once it is turgid no more water can enter. A red cell has **only a membrane**. Nothing limits the water coming in, so it swells until the membrane splits.

Pure water is more dilute than the cytoplasm, so water moves into the cell by osmosis through its selectively permeable membrane. The cell swells and bursts: **lysis**. In the body this does not happen, because the kidneys keep the plasma at the same concentration as the cytoplasm.

noteBlocks.stem: A drip puts liquid straight into a patient's blood, so it is never pure water. Explain what pure water would do to the patient's red blood cells. [3]

steps.working: Pure water is more dilute than the cytoplasm of the red cells, so water would move into them by osmosis, across the selectively permeable membrane.
steps.decision: First the process and its direction: from the dilute water into the more concentrated cytoplasm.

steps.working: The red cells would swell and burst: this is lysis.
steps.decision: Then what happens, with the word the scheme gives its own mark to.

steps.working: They burst because an animal cell has no cell wall to stop more water coming in.
steps.decision: Then the reason. A plant cell in the same water only becomes turgid, because its wall stops more water entering.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why does a red blood cell burst in pure water when a plant cell does not?
options: It has no cell wall to limit the entry of water
Its membrane is not permeable to water
noteBlocks.answer: It has no cell wall to limit the entry of water
noteBlocks.explain: Both cells take in water by osmosis in pure water. The plant cell's wall stops the swelling once the cell is turgid; the red cell has only a membrane, so nothing stops the water, as step 3 of the worked answer said. The missing nucleus plays no part, and the membrane does let water through.

twin.prompt: A plant cell and a red blood cell are both put in pure water. Which one ends up turgid?
twin.explain: Only a cell with a wall can become turgid: the wall pushes back once the cell is full. The red cell has no wall, so it keeps swelling until it bursts.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because the red cell takes in water too, but with no wall to push back it keeps swelling and bursts instead of becoming turgid.
It tempts because both cells take in water by osmosis, but turgid means full and pressing on a wall, and only the plant cell has one.
It tempts because the missing nucleus is the red cell's best-known feature, but it has nothing to do with water entering or the cell bursting.

optionNotes.option: Its membrane is not permeable to water
optionNotes.why: It tempts because a cell that bursts sounds sealed, but the membrane lets water in by osmosis, which is exactly why the cell swells.

noteBlocks.md: An **artery** carries blood away from the heart at **high pressure**, so its wall is thick, with **muscle and elastic fibres**, and its lumen is small. A **vein** carries blood back towards the heart at **low pressure**: its wall is thinner, with less muscle, its lumen is large, and it has **valves**.

A **capillary** has a wall only **one cell thick**, and the wall is permeable, so materials are exchanged between the blood and the tissues. Summer 2025 examiners found fewer candidates could name the capillary as the vessel with this wall.

noteBlocks.stem: Explain why the wall of an artery contains elastic fibres. [2]

steps.working: Each heartbeat pushes blood into the artery at high pressure.
steps.decision: Start from what the wall has to cope with: blood arriving in surges, straight from the heart.

steps.working: The elastic fibres let the wall stretch as the blood surges in and then recoil, so the artery withstands the pressure.
steps.decision: Then the structure doing that job. Stretch and recoil is the idea to write; 'strong' on its own describes the wall without explaining it.

noteBlocks.prompt: An artery wall stretches and then recoils with every heartbeat. Which part of the wall lets it do that?
noteBlocks.explain: Stretching and springing back is what elastic fibres do, as step 2 of the worked answer showed: each surge of high-pressure blood stretches the artery wall, and the fibres recoil. Valves belong to veins, and a wall one cell thick belongs to a capillary.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because valves open and shut with the flow, but valves belong to veins, and arteries have none along their length.
It tempts because a thin wall sounds stretchy, but a wall one cell thick is a capillary's, and it could never withstand the artery's pressure.

twin.prompt: Which vessel's wall has elastic fibres that stretch and recoil with every heartbeat?
twin.explain: Only arteries take the heart's high-pressure surges, so their walls stretch and recoil. A vein's blood is at low pressure, and a capillary wall is one cell thick, with no fibres at all.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because a vein wall holds some elastic fibres too, but far fewer, and its low-pressure blood arrives with no surge to stretch it.
It tempts because capillaries carry the same blood, but a capillary wall is a single layer of cells, with no fibres to stretch.

noteBlocks.caption: Blood moving towards the heart pushes the flaps flat; blood flowing back fills them, and the valve shuts.

noteBlocks.md: By the time blood reaches a vein it has passed through the capillaries, and its pressure is low. The muscles around the vein squeeze it along, and between squeezes the blood could slip backwards.

That is what the **valves** are for: blood flowing backwards fills their flaps and shuts them, so blood can only travel **towards the heart**. An artery needs no valves: the heart keeps its pressure high.

noteBlocks.stem: Blood in a leg vein starts to flow backwards between two squeezes of the leg muscles. Describe what the valve in the vein does, and explain why it is needed. [2]

steps.working: The backflowing blood fills the flaps of the valve and pushes them together, so the valve shuts.
steps.decision: Describe first: what the flaps do when the flow reverses.

steps.working: Blood in a vein is at low pressure, so without valves it could reverse between squeezes; the shut valve keeps it moving one way.
steps.decision: Then explain why: low pressure is the reason a vein needs valves at all.

noteBlocks.prompt: Valves in a vein stop the blood flowing ______.
noteBlocks.explain: Blood in a vein is at low pressure, so between squeezes it could slip back the way it came. When it starts to, it fills the valve's flaps and shuts them, as step 1 of the worked answer described. So the valves stop the blood flowing backwards.

twin.prompt: Blood in a vein can only travel towards the ______.
twin.explain: Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure, and the valves let it move only that way.

noteBlocks.md: To find how much a drawing is enlarged, use **magnification = drawn size ÷ real size**. Put both lengths in the same unit first: cells are measured in micrometres, and 1 mm is 1000 µm. The answer has no unit; write it with a × in front.
To compare two counts from one field of view, divide: 'how many times more' is the larger count divided by the smaller.

noteBlocks.stem:
(a) A white blood cell 14 µm across is drawn 70 mm across. Calculate the magnification of the drawing. [3]
(b) In one field of view there are 180 red blood cells and 4 white blood cells. How many times more red cells are there? [2]

steps.decision: Convert the drawing into micrometres first, the unit the real cell is measured in.

steps.working: magnification = 70 000 ÷ 14
steps.decision: Drawn size over real size, in that order. Upside down it gives a number smaller than 1, a warning sign in itself.
No unit: a magnification compares two lengths. Write the × in front.
For (b), 'how many times more' means the larger count divided by the smaller.

steps.working: 45 times as many red cells as white cells
steps.decision: Say what the number means; the second mark is for the value.

noteBlocks.prompt: A drawing of a platelet is 20 mm across. The real platelet is 2.5 µm across. What is the magnification? Give the number only.
noteBlocks.explain: Convert first, as the worked steps did: 20 mm is 20 000 µm. Then drawn size ÷ real size is 20 000 ÷ 2.5, which is 8000, written ×8000. Dividing 20 by 2.5 without converting gives 8, a thousand times too small.

twin.prompt: A student draws a white blood cell 48 mm wide. The real cell is 15 µm wide. What is the magnification? Give the number only.
twin.explain: 48 mm is 48 000 µm, and 48 000 ÷ 15 is 3200: ×3200. Convert before you divide.

noteBlocks.md: **A matching exercise.** Three parts of blood, each joined to its job, for [3]. Platelets have two jobs to link, fibrinogen to fibrin and clotting; in Summer 2025 many candidates linked only one.

**A tick table of vessels.** Features down the side, artery, vein and capillary across the top, up to [6]. Tick one box a row unless the feature is shared: muscle and elastic fibres are in arteries and veins (Summer 2022).
**Counting a smear.** Count one kind of cell in the photograph, then scale up by the ratio the question gives: the white cells counted, times the red cells expected per white cell (Summer 2023).

noteBlocks.stem:
Complete the table by ticking the vessel or vessels that each feature describes. [4]
has valves · has the thickest wall · has the largest lumen · allows exchange with the tissues

steps.working: Has valves: vein.
steps.decision: Valves keep low-pressure blood moving towards the heart, and only veins need them.

steps.working: Has the thickest wall: artery.
steps.decision: It withstands the high pressure of blood straight from the heart.

steps.working: Has the largest lumen: vein.
steps.decision: A thin wall leaves the most room inside. One vessel can take two rows; a feature shared by two vessels takes two ticks.

steps.working: Allows exchange with the tissues: capillary.
steps.decision: Only a permeable wall one cell thick lets materials pass between blood and tissue.

noteBlocks.prompt: A tick table of blood vessels has the row 'has muscle and elastic fibres in its wall'. Which boxes do you tick?
noteBlocks.explain: A shared feature takes two ticks, as the worked table's reasons said. An artery wall and a vein wall both hold muscle and elastic fibres, the artery far more; a capillary wall is a single layer of cells, with neither. So the row takes two ticks.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because the artery has far more muscle and elastic fibres, but a vein's thinner wall still has some, so its box is ticked too.
It tempts to tick every vessel, but a capillary wall is a single layer of cells with no muscle or elastic fibres, and the scheme docks a mark for the extra tick.

twin.prompt: The next row of the tick table reads 'carries blood away from the heart at high pressure'. Which box do you tick?
twin.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, which is why their walls are thickest. Veins carry it back at low pressure, and capillaries exchange materials with the tissues.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because veins are the other large vessel, but they carry blood back to the heart at low pressure.
It tempts because every vessel carries blood, but a capillary's job is exchange with the tissues, through a wall one cell thick.

noteBlocks.md:
Give the job of each part of blood: red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.
Name what the plasma carries, and say where the oxygen travels instead.
Tell a red cell from a white cell, and explain lysis in pure water (Higher).
Match each vessel's wall, lumen and valves to its job, and work out a magnification.

Blood often opens the Foundation paper: a matching exercise for [3], then single marks for the missing nucleus, the biconcave shape, iron and a substance in the plasma. Vessels come as a tick table worth up to [6], or beside double circulation, where naming the capillary is a mark many miss. Higher adds lysis beside osmosis. Stuck: name the part, then give its one job.

workedExamples.stem:
An artery and a vein from the same stained section were both 5 mm across the outside. The table gives the thickness of each wall.
(a) Calculate the width of the lumen of the artery. [2]
(b) Explain how the artery's wall suits the job it does. [2]

data.caption: Two vessels from one stained section

steps.working: wall on both sides = 2 × 1.3 = 2.6 mm
steps.decision: The wall runs all the way round, so a line across the section crosses it twice. Taking it off only once is the usual slip.

steps.working: lumen = 5 − 2.6 = 2.4 mm
steps.decision: Outside width minus both wall thicknesses. The vein, the same size outside, has a lumen of 4.2 mm: the same tube from outside, very different inside.

options: Because the wall is crossed once on the way in and once on the way out
Because the artery wall is thicker than the vein wall
Because the lumen is always half the outside width
whyMenu.explain: A cross-section is a ring: the outside width holds two thicknesses of wall plus the lumen.

steps.working: The wall is thick, with muscle and elastic fibres in it.
steps.decision: Name the structure first. 'Thick' alone describes it; the muscle and elastic fibres are what the scheme lists.

accepted: The wall is thick, with muscle and elastic fibres in it.

steps.working: It withstands the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart, and the elastic fibres let it stretch and recoil with each beat.
steps.decision: Then the job it does. Structure plus function: the function is where the second mark is.

accepted: It withstands the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart, and the elastic fibres let it stretch and recoil with each beat.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 2.4 mm. (b) The wall is thick, with muscle and elastic fibres, so it withstands the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart and stretches and recoils with each beat.

twin.stem: A vein is 4.5 mm across the outside and its wall is 0.4 mm thick. Calculate the width of its lumen, in mm.

workedExamples.stem:
A student draws a red blood cell 32 mm across. The real cell is 8 µm across.
(a) Calculate the magnification of the drawing. [3]
(b) The real cell is a biconcave disc. Explain how this shape helps it take up oxygen. [1]

steps.decision: Both lengths must be in the same unit before you divide. The real cell is in micrometres, so convert the drawing: 1 mm is 1000 µm.

steps.working: magnification = drawn size ÷ real size = 32 000 ÷ 8
steps.decision: Drawn over real, in that order. Upside down it gives a number smaller than 1, a warning sign in itself.

options: Because the drawing is compared with the real cell, both in micrometres
Because the real size is always the bigger number
Because millimetres and micrometres can be divided as they stand
whyMenu.explain: Magnification says how many times bigger the drawing is than the real thing: drawn size over real size, in one unit.

steps.decision: A magnification has no unit: it is a ratio of two lengths. Write it with a × in front.

steps.working: The biconcave shape gives the cell a large surface area, so it absorbs oxygen quickly.
steps.decision: Shape, then what it buys: a large surface area for oxygen to diffuse into. 'Biconcave' alone repeats the question; the surface area is the explanation.

accepted: The biconcave shape gives the cell a large surface area, so it absorbs oxygen quickly.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) ×4000. (b) Its biconcave shape gives a large surface area, so it absorbs oxygen quickly.

items.stem: Before we start, three things you have already met. Which structure is found in an animal cell but NOT in a bacterial cell?

options.text: a nucleus
options.feedback: A nucleus. Keep hold of it: one blood cell is famous for giving its nucleus up.

options.text: a cell membrane
options.feedback: Bacteria have a membrane too. What they lack is a nucleus; their DNA lies loose in the cytoplasm.

options.text: cytoplasm
options.feedback: Every cell has cytoplasm.

options.text: a cell wall
options.feedback: Bacteria do have a wall, though not a cellulose one. Animal cells are the ones without.

items.stem: A cell is put into pure water. Which way does water move?

options.text: into the cell
options.feedback: Into the cell: pure water is the most dilute solution there is.

options.text: out of the cell
options.feedback: Water moves towards the more concentrated solution, and that is the cytoplasm inside the cell.

options.text: neither way
options.feedback: There is no net movement only when the two solutions match. Pure water and cytoplasm do not.

options.text: into the cell, using energy from respiration
options.feedback: The direction is right, but osmosis is free: it needs no energy.

options.text: Molecules spreading from where there are more of them to where there are fewer
options.feedback: Down the gradient. Every exchange in a capillary works this way.

options.text: Molecules being pumped using energy
options.feedback: That is active transport. Diffusion costs nothing.

options.text: Water moving through a membrane
options.feedback: That is osmosis, which is one special case of diffusion.

options.text: Blood being pushed along a vessel
options.feedback: That is the heart's doing, not diffusion.

items.stem: Which component of blood converts fibrinogen to fibrin?
items.skill: Match a component to its function

options.text: platelets
options.feedback: Platelets. Fibrin makes the mesh that traps cells and forms a clot, and then a scab.

options.text: red blood cells
options.feedback: Red cells carry oxygen. Clotting is the platelets' job.

options.text: white blood cells
options.feedback: White cells defend against disease. Summer 2025 examiners recorded that many candidates could not link platelets to their two functions.

options.text: plasma
options.feedback: Plasma is the liquid that carries everything. It contains the fibrinogen, but the platelets do the converting.

items.stem: Which of these is an adaptation of a red blood cell for carrying oxygen?

options.text: It has no nucleus, so there is more room for haemoglobin
options.feedback: No nucleus, more haemoglobin. Summer 2024 examiners found the adaptations surprisingly poorly known.

options.text: It has a large nucleus to control oxygen uptake
options.feedback: A mature red blood cell has no nucleus at all — that is the point.

options.text: It is a cube, which packs tightly in the vessel
options.feedback: It is a biconcave disc: dimpled on both sides, which gives a large surface area.

options.text: It contains fibrin to help it stick to the vessel wall
options.feedback: Fibrin belongs to clotting. A red cell contains haemoglobin.

items.stem: Which substance does blood plasma transport?

options.text: urea
options.feedback: Urea, on its way to the kidneys. Plasma also carries cells, food molecules, carbon dioxide and hormones.

options.text: oxygen
options.feedback: Almost all the oxygen travels inside red blood cells, bound to haemoglobin. Summer 2023 examiners saw oxygen given here and it was not credited.

options.text: haemoglobin
options.feedback: Haemoglobin stays inside the red blood cells; it is not dissolved in the plasma.

options.text: fibrin
options.feedback: Fibrin only forms when a clot is made. Plasma carries the fibrinogen it is made from.

items.stem: Why does an artery have a much smaller lumen than a vein of the same outside width?

options.text: Its wall is far thicker, to withstand high pressure
options.feedback: The wall takes up the space. Thick muscle and elastic fibres are what high-pressure blood needs.

options.text: It carries less blood than a vein
options.feedback: The same blood passes through both. The difference is the wall, not the amount.

options.text: It has valves that take up room
options.feedback: Arteries have no valves. Veins are the ones with valves.

options.text: It is further from the heart
options.feedback: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and the pressure there is high, which is why the wall is thick.

items.stem: Why is a capillary wall only one cell thick?

options.text: So materials can be exchanged quickly with the tissues
options.feedback: Short distance, fast diffusion. Exchange is the whole job of a capillary.

options.text: So the blood can travel faster
options.feedback: Blood actually flows slowly in capillaries, which gives more time for exchange.

options.text: So it can withstand high pressure
options.feedback: A thin wall is the opposite of what withstands pressure. That is the artery's problem.

options.text: So valves can open and close inside it
options.feedback: Capillaries have no valves. Only veins do.

items.stem: Higher Tier. Red blood cells are placed in pure water. What happens, and why?
items.skill: Apply osmosis to an animal cell

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cells burst
options.feedback: Lysis. With no cell wall there is nothing to limit the water entering.

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cells become turgid
options.feedback: Turgid is a plant-cell word: it needs a wall for the contents to press against.

options.text: Water leaves by osmosis and the cells shrink
options.feedback: That happens in a concentrated salt solution. Pure water is more dilute than the cytoplasm, so water moves in.

options.text: Nothing happens, because the cells have no nucleus
options.feedback: The missing nucleus makes no difference to osmosis. The missing cell wall makes all the difference.

parts.stem: Name the vessel that carries blood away from the heart under high pressure.

accepted: an artery

parts.workedSolution: An artery.

parts.stem: Name the vessel with valves that carries blood back towards the heart under low pressure.

accepted: a vein

parts.workedSolution: A vein.

parts.stem: Name the vessel whose permeable wall is one cell thick, where materials are exchanged with the tissues.

accepted: a capillary

parts.workedSolution: A capillary.

commonErrors.feedback: Arteries and veins have thick multi-layered walls. The one-cell-thick vessel where exchange happens is the capillary. Summer 2025 examiners recorded that fewer candidates could name it than could describe what it does.

parts.stem: The artery is 6.0 mm across the outside and its wall is 1.5 mm thick. Calculate the width of its lumen, in mm.
hints: The wall goes all the way round, so how many thicknesses lie across the vessel?
parts.workedSolution: The wall is crossed twice, so it accounts for 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 mm. The lumen is 6.0 − 3.0 = 3.0 mm.

commonErrors.feedback: The wall has been subtracted once. A cross-section is a ring, so the outside width contains two thicknesses of wall plus the lumen.

hints: Put both lengths in the same unit first. There are 1000 µm in 1 mm.
parts.workedSolution: 42 mm is 42000 µm. Magnification = drawn size ÷ real size = 42000 ÷ 7 = ×6000. A magnification is a ratio, so it carries no unit.

commonErrors.feedback: Millimetres have been divided by micrometres. Convert the drawing to micrometres first: 1 mm is 1000 µm.
Real size has been divided by drawn size. Magnification is drawn ÷ real, and a magnified drawing always gives a number bigger than one.

hints: Divide the larger count by the smaller one.
parts.workedSolution: 240 ÷ 3 = 80 times as many.

commonErrors.feedback: The counts have been divided the wrong way round. 'How many times more red cells' means red divided by white.

parts.stem: A runner's red blood cell count rose from 5.0 million per mm³ to 5.6 million per mm³ after a month training at altitude. Calculate the percentage increase.
hints: Divide by the count she started with.
parts.workedSolution: The increase is 5.6 − 5.0 = 0.6 million per mm³, and 0.6 ÷ 5.0 × 100 = 12.0%.

commonErrors.feedback: The increase has been divided by the final count. A percentage increase is measured against the count at the start.

parts.stem: Suggest how the extra red blood cells help her to run faster.

accepted: more red cells carry more oxygen to her muscles, so more aerobic respiration can take place and more energy is released

scheme.for: more red cells carry more oxygen to the muscles
so more aerobic respiration takes place and more energy is released

hints: What do red cells carry, and what is it used for?
parts.workedSolution: More red blood cells means more haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried to her muscles. More aerobic respiration can take place there, releasing more energy, so she can work harder before her muscles have to respire anaerobically.

parts.stem:
Describe the structure of an artery, a vein and a capillary, and explain how each one is suited to the job it does.
The quality of your written communication is marked here too, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; everything set out in a clear and sensible order; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; an order you can follow, though it is not held right through; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; ideas in an order that is hard to follow; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave what you meant unclear.

indicativeContent.point: an artery has a thick wall containing muscle and elastic fibres
which withstands the high pressure of blood carried away from the heart, and stretches and recoils with each beat
an artery has a small lumen; a vein has a large one
a vein has a thin wall with little muscle, because blood in it is at low pressure
a vein has valves, which prevent backflow and keep the blood moving towards the heart
a capillary wall is one cell thick, so substances have only a short distance to diffuse
and it is permeable, which allows the exchange of materials with the tissues

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Answers that list features without saying what each one is for cap at Band B: the specification asks for structures related to functions. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Three vessels, and for each one a structure and the job it suits — that is six points already.
The words that lift an answer to Band A are lumen, elastic fibres, valves, backflow and permeable.
parts.workedSolution: An artery has a thick wall containing muscle and elastic fibres. It carries blood away from the heart at high pressure, and the thick wall withstands that pressure while the elastic fibres let it stretch and recoil with every beat. Its lumen is small. A vein has a much thinner wall with little muscle, because the blood in it is at low pressure by the time it returns, and its lumen is large. A vein also has valves, which shut if the blood starts to flow backwards, so it can only travel towards the heart. A capillary has a wall only one cell thick, so oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide have a very short distance to diffuse, and the wall is permeable, which allows materials to be exchanged with the tissues.

pattern.regex: ^(?![\s\S]*(permeable|porous|one cell thick|single cell|a cell thick|cell thick|exchange))[\s\S]*$

commonErrors.feedback: The capillary is the vessel most answers thin out. Two things earn its marks: a wall one cell thick, and a permeable wall that lets materials be exchanged with the tissues.

parts.stem: Red blood cells are placed in distilled water. Describe and explain what happens to them.

accepted: water enters the cells by osmosis because the distilled water is more dilute than the cytoplasm, the cells swell, and because they have no cell wall to limit the water entering they burst

scheme.for: water enters the cells by osmosis, because the distilled water is more dilute than the cytoplasm
they have no cell wall to limit the entry of water, so they burst (lysis)

hints: Which way does the water go, and why?
The last mark is for the structure a plant cell has and this one does not.
parts.workedSolution: Distilled water is more dilute than the cytoplasm inside the red blood cells, so water moves into them by osmosis through their selectively permeable membranes. The cells swell, and because an animal cell has no cell wall to limit the entry of water, they keep swelling until the membrane splits and they burst. This is called lysis.

parts.stem: Name the vessel drawn on the left, which has the thickest wall and the smallest lumen.

accepted: an artery

parts.workedSolution: An artery.

commonErrors.feedback: A vein has the thin wall and the large lumen. Thick wall, small lumen, high pressure: that is an artery.

parts.stem: Describe two ways the wall of a vein differs from the wall of an artery.

accepted: the vein wall is thinner, and it has valves inside it

any: wall of a vein is thinner
wall of the vein is thinner
wall of an artery is thicker

scheme.for: the vein wall is thinner, with less muscle and fewer elastic fibres

scheme.examinerNote: A larger lumen is also credited, but it is a feature of the vessel rather than of the wall.

hints: One about how thick it is, one about something inside it that an artery does not have.
parts.workedSolution: The vein's wall is much thinner, with less muscle and fewer elastic fibres in it, and it contains valves, which an artery does not have.

commonErrors.feedback: Only veins have valves along their length. Getting that the wrong way round loses the mark it sits with.

parts.stem: Explain how a capillary is adapted for the exchange of materials with the tissues.

accepted: its wall is only one cell thick, so substances have only a short distance to diffuse, and the wall is permeable so dissolved substances can pass through it into the tissues

scheme.for: the wall is one cell thick
so substances have only a short distance to diffuse
and the wall is permeable, so dissolved substances can pass through it

hints: Structure, then what the structure allows.
Three marks means three separate ideas, not one idea in three ways.
parts.workedSolution: A capillary's wall is only one cell thick, so oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide have only a short distance to diffuse between the blood and the tissue cells. The wall is also permeable, so dissolved substances can pass through it. Together with the slow flow of blood through capillaries, that makes them very good at exchange.

commonErrors.feedback: Withstanding pressure is the artery's job. A capillary is built the opposite way: as thin and permeable as possible, for exchange.

findTheMistake.stem:
Sinéad is asked: 'A drawing of a red blood cell is 42 mm across. The real cell is 7 µm across. Calculate the magnification. [3]'
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The equation in line 1 is exactly right. Line 2 divides millimetres by micrometres, which is like dividing miles by inches: the two lengths have to be in the same unit first. 42 mm is 42000 µm.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of the three: the method line stands, and in a scheme that gives a mark for the equation it would be credited. The conversion mark and the answer mark go together. A useful habit is to write the unit beside every number as you substitute — the moment you see "mm ÷ µm" on the page, the conversion asks for itself.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'Describe how oxygen gets from the blood into a working muscle cell. [3]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Oxygen is released from the haemoglobin in the red blood cells.
It passes out through the wall of a vein into the muscle.
That wall is only one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is short.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 3 are right, and line 3 even describes the vessel correctly. But a wall one cell thick belongs to a capillary: a vein's wall is thicker, and exchange with the tissues happens through the capillaries. Summer 2025 examiners found fewer candidates could name that vessel as a capillary.
correction: Oxygen is released from the haemoglobin in the red blood cells.
It passes out through the wall of a capillary into the muscle.
That wall is only one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is short.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks of the three: the mark for naming where the exchange happens is the one lost. Tie the feature to its vessel: a permeable wall one cell thick, exchanging materials with the tissues, is always a capillary.

prompts.prompt: Give three adaptations of a red blood cell.
prompts.answer: Biconcave shape for a large surface area, no nucleus so there is more room inside, and packed with haemoglobin, which contains iron.

prompts.prompt: Name three substances carried in the plasma — and one that is not.
prompts.answer: Food molecules, carbon dioxide, hormones and urea are carried in the plasma. Oxygen is not: it travels inside the red blood cells.

prompts.prompt: Describe the wall of an artery and say why it is like that.
prompts.answer: Thick, with muscle and elastic fibres, to withstand the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart and to stretch and recoil with each beat.

prompts.prompt: Describe a vein, and say what its valves do.
prompts.answer: A thin wall with little muscle and a large lumen; the valves prevent backflow, so blood at low pressure can only travel towards the heart.

prompts.prompt: Higher Tier: what happens to red blood cells put in distilled water, and why?
prompts.answer: Water enters by osmosis and they burst, because an animal cell has no cell wall to limit the entry of water. This is lysis.

prompts.prompt: How do you calculate a magnification from a drawing?
prompts.answer: Magnification = drawn size ÷ real size, with both lengths converted to the same unit first. It has no unit.

prompts.prompt: What is the job of each of the four parts of blood?
prompts.answer: Red cells carry oxygen, white cells defend, platelets clot the blood, plasma transports.
